newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli rate cut forecast in second quarter.
newsitem.headline: Israeli rate cut forecast in second quarter.

text.p: Israeli interest rates will fall by 0.5 percentage point during the second quarter due to a slowing economy but will hold steady in the third quarter, Israel Discount Bank said in a report released on Tuesday.

"The rise in the public's inflationary expectations for the coming year into the upper end of the (government's) inflation target and the growing possibility that the 1997 budget deficit will exceed its target will result in stable interest rates in the third quarter," Discount said.

The Bank of Israel's base rate has been at 13.9 percent since the end of February after declining 3.1 percentage points in the previous seven months. Inflationary expectations in the bond market are currently around 9.6 percent, compared with the government target of seven to 10 percent.
Discount said it expected consumer prices to rise by 9.5 to 10 percent over the next 12 months.

The bank said that based on first-quarter figures it expected the budget deficit to exceed its full-year target by two to three billion shekels, or 0.7 percentage of gross domestic product. The Treasury's target is 2.8 percent of GDP.

"This overshooting, in addition to the lag of about one billion shekels in forecasted income from privatisation, will lead to increased domestic borrowing by the government in the bond market during the second half of 1997," Discount concluded.

It said inflation fell to an average monthly rise of 0.5 percent in first-quarter 1997, which it said was due to the Israeli shekel's strength relative to the foreign currency basket to which it is linked. This was offset by a relatively steep increase in housing prices.
The bank said the level and composition of capital imports this year pointed to continued strength of the shekel.

"The growth in the weighting of capital imports that are unaffected by interest rate differentials between Israel and overseas, such as foreign investment and overseas public offerings by Israeli companies, increase the chances of continued supply in the forex market in coming months," Discount said.
It estimated that in the first quarter the Bank of Israel bought $4 billion in foreign currency.
